title: Two Brothers and Two Ways
summary: Cain murders Abel after God accepts Abel’s offering; Cain’s line builds cities and violence, while Seth’s birth renews the promised seed and worship.
historicalContext: Genesis 4 follows the family of Adam and Eve into the world outside Eden. Life now unfolds east of the garden, under the curse on the ground and the promise of a coming Seed (3:15–24). The first sons take up the two basic occupations of early human life, farming and herding, and the first recorded act of worship centers on offerings brought to the LORD. The sacrifices of 3:21 and the clothing God provided stand in the background, suggesting that worship by sacrifice had already been made known. The chapter covers many generations quickly: the founding of a settlement, the rise of herding, music, and metalwork, the first instance of polygamy, and a widening practice of revenge. It closes by returning to Adam’s household, where the birth of Seth and Enosh marks the continuation of a worshiping line through which the promise would be carried.
literaryContext: The chapter mirrors Genesis 3 at many points: sin crouching and desiring, God’s searching question, a denial, a curse involving the ground, an act of protection, and a movement eastward away from the divine presence. The word “brother” recurs throughout the Cain and Abel account, pressing home the horror of fratricide. The narrative alternates birth and bloodshed: births in verses 1–2, murder in verses 3–16, a family line in verses 17–22, Lamech’s boast in verses 23–24, and a new birth in verses 25–26. Cain’s line is traced to the seventh generation, Lamech, whose vengeance contrasts with the seventh from Adam through Seth, Enoch, who walked with God (5:21–24). The chapter thus prepares for the genealogy of Genesis 5 and the corruption that brings the flood in Genesis 6, setting two ways of life side by side.
themes: Worship on God’s terms or our own
Sin crouching at the door and the call to master it
The first fruit of the enmity foretold in Eden
Divine justice joined with restraining mercy
Culture without God and the escalation of violence
The preserved seed and the renewal of worship

outline.title: The First Births Outside Eden
outline.summary: Eve bears Cain with hope in the LORD’s promise and then Abel, and the brothers take up the work of the field and the flock.

outline.title: Two Offerings and a Warning
outline.summary: God regards Abel and his offering but not Cain’s, and He reasons with the angry Cain about doing well and mastering sin.

outline.title: The First Murder and Its Sentence
outline.summary: Cain kills his brother, denies responsibility, and is cursed to wander, yet God sets a mark to restrain those who would kill him.

outline.title: The Line of Cain
outline.summary: Cain’s descendants found a city and develop herding, music, and metalwork, while Lamech takes two wives and boasts of limitless vengeance.

outline.title: Seth and the Calling on the LORD
outline.summary: God appoints another seed in place of Abel, and in the days of Enos people begin to call upon the name of the LORD.

verses.bibleText: And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain, and said, I have gotten a man from the LORD.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The story of humanity outside Eden begins with a birth. “Adam knew Eve his wife” uses the ordinary Hebrew verb for knowing to describe the intimate union of husband and wife, a union that is personal and covenantal rather than merely physical. The first command of blessing, “Be fruitful, and multiply” (1:28), continues even after the fall. Death has been pronounced, yet life still comes into the world, and Eve becomes in fact what Adam had named her, “the mother of all living” (3:20).

Eve’s words at Cain’s birth are striking. She is the first person in Scripture recorded as speaking the covenant name, the LORD. The Hebrew reads very compactly: “I have gotten a man, the LORD,” or “with the LORD.” The little word that stands before the divine name also stands before Cain’s name earlier in the verse, which makes it possible that Eve was saying more than that God had helped her. Fresh from hearing that the woman’s seed would bruise the serpent’s head (3:15), she appears to have hoped that this very child was the promised Deliverer. Her joy was real, and her faith in the promise was sound, but her timing was mistaken. The son she welcomed as the answer to the curse would become the first murderer.

The name Cain sounds like the verb Eve uses, “gotten” or “acquired.” The wordplay foreshadows a man who will be marked by possession and self-assertion. Eve’s calling her infant “a man” is also unexpected, perhaps an echo of the first man’s delight in the woman (2:23): woman once came from man, and now man comes from woman, and both come from God (1 Corinthians 11:12).

The verse teaches patience in hope. God’s promise was certain, yet it would unfold over long ages until “the fulness of the time was come” and God sent forth His Son, “made of a woman” (Galatians 4:4). Believers who long for the Lord’s return share something of Eve’s eagerness, and they too must learn to wait without abandoning the promise when early hopes are disappointed.

wordNotes.term: קָנִיתִי אִישׁ אֶת־יְהוָה (qaniti ish et-YHWH) — I have gotten a man from the LORD
wordNotes.explanation: The verb qanah means to acquire or obtain and forms a wordplay with the name Cain (qayin). The particle et before the divine name may mean “with” (with the LORD’s help) or may mark the LORD as standing in apposition to “a man.” The second reading would express Eve’s hope that her son was the promised Seed. The ambiguity fits the moment: Eve credits the LORD and clings to His promise, though she misreads its timing.

verses.bibleText: And she again bare his brother Abel. And Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abel’s birth is reported without the usual “and she conceived,” and without any comment from his mother. The Hebrew says simply that she “added to bear,” which some take as a hint that the boys were twins, though the text does not require it. What the narrative emphasizes instead is relationship. Abel is introduced as “his brother,” and that identity will be repeated through the following verses until it becomes an accusation: the man Cain killed was his own brother.

The name Abel (hevel) means breath or vapor, the same word the Preacher uses for what is fleeting and insubstantial (Ecclesiastes 1:2). Whether Eve chose it from weariness with the hardships of life or simply as a name, the reader soon feels its weight. Abel’s life will pass like a breath. He never speaks in the narrative, and he leaves no descendants, yet Scripture remembers him as righteous and as one who “being dead yet speaketh” through the testimony of his faith (Hebrews 11:4).

The brothers divide the two great labors of the early world. Abel becomes “a keeper of sheep,” and Cain “a tiller of the ground,” the work given to Adam in 3:23. Neither occupation is morally superior. Both carry forward the charge to have dominion and to work the earth, and both would later be honored among God’s people. The difference between the brothers will lie in the heart, not in the calling. Pastoral care of flocks does, however, place Abel near the animals from which sacrifices were drawn, and that detail prepares for the offerings that follow.

The reversal of birth order also begins here. The younger brother, not the elder, will become the model of acceptable worship, a pattern that recurs with Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, and Ephraim. God’s choices do not follow human expectations of rank.

wordNotes.term: הֶבֶל (hevel) — Abel
wordNotes.explanation: The name means breath, vapor, or a puff of air, and elsewhere describes what is brief and passing, as in the refrain “vanity of vanities.” The narrator does not explain the name, but Abel’s short life gives it a poignant fitness. Its meaning should not be pressed to suggest that Abel himself was worthless; Scripture honors him as righteous.

verses.bibleText: And in process of time it came to pass, that Cain brought of the fruit of the ground an offering unto the LORD.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“In process of time” renders a Hebrew expression meaning “at the end of days.” It marks a considerable but unspecified interval, perhaps the close of a season such as harvest. Both brothers come at the same time with their offerings, which suggests a shared, recognized occasion of worship rather than two spontaneous impulses. The family outside Eden still approaches the LORD and expects to be heard.

The chapter does not mention an altar, but sacrifice implies one, and the next recorded offering, Noah’s, is made on an altar (8:20). Worship by sacrifice did not arise as a human invention. When God clothed Adam and Eve with skins (3:21), an animal died to cover their shame, and the practice of bringing an offering for sin appears to have been taught from that time. Later Scripture confirms that Abel offered “by faith” (Hebrews 11:4), and faith responds to what God has spoken (Romans 10:17). If Cain and Abel had received no instruction, God’s different response to their offerings would seem arbitrary, and Cain never protests that he did not know what was required.

Cain brings “of the fruit of the ground.” The word for offering, minchah, is broad and can describe gifts of produce or animals. Later law would welcome grain offerings in their place (Leviticus 2), so produce was not in itself unworthy. Yet the narrator says nothing about the first or the best, and the setting is a sinner’s approach to a holy God after the fall. Cain came as a man who considered himself in good standing, bringing what his own hands had produced from the cursed ground. He offered acknowledgment without confession.

Cain’s worship looked religious and outwardly correct. Its fault lay beneath the surface, in the choice to approach God on his own terms. That danger did not end with Cain. Every form of religion that seeks to satisfy God with self-chosen gifts while bypassing the sacrifice God has provided follows “the way of Cain” (Jude 1:11).

wordNotes.term: מִנְחָה (minchah) — an offering
wordNotes.explanation: The word means a gift or tribute presented to a superior. In the Levitical laws it usually names the grain offering, but here it describes both Cain’s produce and Abel’s animals (verse 4). The term itself does not decide why one offering was accepted. That answer comes from the narrator’s details, God’s words to Cain, and the New Testament’s explanation that Abel offered by faith.

wordNotes.term: מִקֵּץ יָמִים (miqqets yamim) — in process of time
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “at the end of days,” the phrase denotes the close of a period whose length is not stated. Days can sometimes stand for a year in Hebrew usage, but the phrase here simply indicates that time had passed and that both brothers came to worship on the same occasion.

verses.bibleText: And Abel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. And the LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abel “also brought,” and the narrator immediately describes his gift with care: “the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof.” The firstborn and the fat were the choicest portions, the parts later reserved for the LORD in Israel’s worship (Exodus 13:12; Leviticus 3:16). Abel gave from the first and the best rather than from whatever was at hand. More importantly, his offering involved the death of a substitute. In bringing a slain lamb, Abel confessed that he was a sinner whose life was forfeit and that he looked to God’s provision for covering, as his parents had been covered in the garden.

Hebrews explains the difference: “By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, by which he obtained witness that he was righteous” (Hebrews 11:4). Abel’s obedience grew out of trust. His lamb had no power to earn favor; its worth lay in the reliance it expressed on the One whom God would provide. Scripture later states that “without shedding of blood is no remission” (Hebrews 9:22) and that the blood makes atonement for life (Leviticus 17:11). Abel’s firstling looked ahead, however dimly, to “the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world” (John 1:29).

The order of the final clause matters: “the LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering.” God regarded the worshiper first and then the gift. Offerings are never detached from the person who brings them. A heart of faith gave Abel’s sacrifice its acceptability, and the sacrifice gave that faith its proper expression. The text does not say how God made His regard known. Later accounts in which fire from the LORD consumed an accepted offering (Leviticus 9:24; 1 Kings 18:38) suggest one possibility, and the brothers clearly perceived the difference.

Abel thus stands at the head of the long line of the faithful in Hebrews 11. He is the first person in Scripture to be called righteous, and his righteousness rested on faith in God’s appointed sacrifice. The same way remains open: the sinner who comes trusting in Christ’s offering is accepted “in the beloved” (Ephesians 1:6).

wordNotes.term: שָׁעָה (sha‘ah) — had respect
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to look at with attention, to regard with favor. It describes God’s gracious acceptance rather than mere notice. Notably, the LORD regards Abel himself before his offering, showing that the worshiper’s heart and the gift belong together. The same verb is used when people look in trust to their Maker.

wordNotes.term: מִבְּכֹרוֹת צֹאנוֹ וּמֵחֶלְבֵהֶן (mibbekhorot tso’no umechelvehen) — of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof
wordNotes.explanation: The firstborn and the fat were the best portions, later claimed by the LORD in Israel’s sacrificial law. Abel’s gift was costly and slain, the kind of offering that confessed sin and looked to God’s provision of a substitute.

verses.bibleText: But unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect. And Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect.” Once again person and gift are joined. God did not reject the produce while approving the man; He withheld His favor from both, because the gift expressed the heart of the giver. Cain’s offering lacked the faith that made Abel’s acceptable, and it lacked the confession of need that a slain sacrifice embodied.

Cain’s reaction reveals what lay beneath his worship. “Cain was very wroth,” literally “it burned to Cain exceedingly.” Anger flared at once, with no pause for self-examination, no question about what he had done amiss, and no prayer for pardon. His resentment ran in two directions: against God, who had not approved him, and against Abel, whom God had accepted. Wounded pride rather than sorrow for sin governed his response.

“His countenance fell” describes the outward sign of an inward state. His face, downcast and darkened, showed sullen displeasure. In Scripture a lifted or shining face signals favor and peace (Numbers 6:25–26), and Cain had lost both. He made no attempt to hide his feelings, though he would soon try to hide his deeds.

This verse offers a searching test for every worshiper. When God does not grant the approval we expect, the response exposes whether our worship aimed at Him or at our own standing. Cain shows the path of a heart that hardens under correction. The opposite path is shown by David, who received rebuke and said, “I have sinned against the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:13).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּחַר לְקַיִן מְאֹד (wayyichar leqayin me’od) — Cain was very wroth
wordNotes.explanation: The idiom means “it burned to Cain greatly,” picturing anger as heat rising within. The same expression describes Jonah’s sullen anger when God showed mercy to Nineveh. In both cases the anger is directed at God’s way of dealing with people and is gently questioned by God Himself.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּפְּלוּ פָּנָיו (wayyippelu panaw) — his countenance fell
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “his face fell,” the phrase describes a downcast, glowering expression. It sets up God’s promise in verse 7 of a “lifting up” if Cain does well, contrasting the fallen face of resentment with the lifted face of acceptance.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD said unto Cain, Why art thou wroth? and why is thy countenance fallen?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God does not leave Cain alone with his anger. He speaks to him directly, showing that the LORD continued to address people after the expulsion from Eden. As He had come to Adam with questions (3:9–11), He now comes to Cain: “Why art thou wroth? and why is thy countenance fallen?”

These questions are not requests for information. God knows the heart. They are invitations to self-examination. If Cain would answer honestly, he would have to admit that his anger had no just cause and that the reason for God’s displeasure lay in himself. The rejection of the offering was not yet the rejection of the man. God was offering Cain another opportunity before sin took its next step.

The tenderness of this approach stands out. Cain had brought an offering in the wrong spirit and then turned sullen when it was refused, yet God reasons with him as a father reasons with a resentful son. Divine patience goes ahead of judgment throughout Scripture: “Come now, and let us reason together” (Isaiah 1:18). The Lord “is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9).

wordNotes.term: לָמָּה (lammah) — why
wordNotes.explanation: The interrogative asks for a reason. Repeated twice, it presses Cain to examine the cause of his anger and his fallen face. Divine questions in Genesis typically draw out confession rather than supply God with facts He lacks.

verses.bibleText: If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God’s words to Cain form one of the most difficult sentences in Genesis, yet their main thrust is clear. Two possibilities stand before him. “If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted?” The Hebrew for “accepted” is a single word meaning “lifting up.” It answers the fallen face of verse 6. If Cain turns and does what is right, his face will be lifted, his guilt borne away, and his standing with God restored. The door to acceptance had not closed. The very God who had refused the offering now urges Cain to come again in the right way.

“Doing well” here includes more than conduct in general. It points back to the worship just described. Cain had been shown the appointed way of approach, and he could still come with a heart of faith and an offering that confessed his need. Right worship and right living are joined throughout Scripture; the person reconciled to God by His provision will also learn to do justly and love mercy (Micah 6:8).

The second possibility is grim: “if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door.” Sin is pictured as a wild animal crouching at the entrance of a dwelling, waiting for the moment to spring. The Hebrew participle for “lieth” is masculine, though the word for sin is feminine, which suits a personified beast more than an abstract idea. Peter uses a similar image of the adversary as a lion seeking whom he may devour (1 Peter 5:8). Some have proposed reading the word as “sin offering,” a sacrificial animal lying near at hand for Cain to bring. The idea is attractive, but the grammar and the following clause favor the picture of sin as a predator.

“Unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.” The wording deliberately echoes 3:16, where the same rare word for desire and the same verb for rule appear. As the pronouns are best understood, sin longs to seize and control Cain, and Cain is called to master it. The command carries both warning and hope. Sin is powerful but not irresistible; Cain is responsible and is told he can prevail. No one is forced into evil.

The gospel supplies what Cain refused. The power to master sin comes from the God who offers acceptance first. “Sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace” (Romans 6:14). Those who receive Christ’s sacrifice also receive His strength to resist what crouches at the door (James 4:7).

wordNotes.term: שְׂאֵת (se’et) — shalt thou not be accepted
wordNotes.explanation: The noun comes from nasa’, “to lift up, bear.” It answers Cain’s fallen face: doing well would bring a lifted countenance, a sign of acceptance and peace. The same verb is used for bearing or forgiving iniquity, so the word hints that acceptance includes the removal of guilt, which God alone provides.

wordNotes.term: חַטָּאת רֹבֵץ (chatta’t rovets) — sin lieth at the door
wordNotes.explanation: Rovets describes an animal crouching or lying down. Because the participle is masculine while chatta’t is feminine, the phrase likely personifies sin as a beast lying in wait at the doorway. The following words, “unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him,” echo Genesis 3:16 and portray sin’s longing to overpower Cain and his duty to master it.

verses.bibleText: And Cain talked with Abel his brother: and it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Cain does not answer God. Instead, “Cain talked with Abel his brother.” The Hebrew says literally “Cain said to Abel,” and the content of his words is missing from the traditional text. Ancient translations such as the Greek version supply “Let us go into the field,” which fits the narrative well whether or not it was part of the original wording. Either way, the silence is telling. Cain’s reply to God’s warning comes in words and deeds aimed at his brother, with no confession offered to the LORD.

“When they were in the field” places the crime away from others, in open country where no one would see. Cain may have planned the act. It may also be that resentment smoldered through conversation until it burst into violence. Either way, the sin that had crouched at the door now leaps. In one generation the alienation that began in Eden has grown from hiding among the trees to shedding a brother’s blood.

“Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him.” The word “brother” appears twice in this verse, and the repetition is deliberate. Cain kills not an enemy or a stranger but the son of his own mother. John explains the motive: Cain “was of that wicked one, and slew his brother. And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother’s righteous” (1 John 3:12). Abel’s acceptance exposed Cain’s self-chosen worship, and Cain silenced the witness rather than change his course.

Here the enmity announced in Eden (3:15) breaks into history. The conflict between the serpent and the woman’s seed now appears within the human family itself, as one son takes the side of the deceiver against the brother who walked by faith. Jesus calls the devil “a murderer from the beginning” (John 8:44), and Cain’s act reveals the character of the one whose spirit he had chosen to follow. The great controversy between Christ and Satan is not an abstraction; it shows itself in hatred of the righteous, in religious violence, and in the persecution that Jesus said would come upon His followers (Matthew 23:35; John 16:2).

The first death recorded in Scripture is therefore a murder, and the first martyr dies over worship. Yet Abel’s faith was not defeated. God would hear his blood, honor his testimony, and finally answer it in the blood of Jesus, which “speaketh better things than that of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24).

wordNotes.term: וַיֹּאמֶר קַיִן (wayyo’mer qayin) — and Cain talked
wordNotes.explanation: The verb normally introduces speech, but the words that follow are not given in the traditional Hebrew text. Ancient Greek, Samaritan, and Syriac renderings supply “Let us go into the field.” The gap highlights that Cain answered God’s warning by turning to his brother instead of responding to the LORD.

wordNotes.term: אָחִיו (achiw) — his brother
wordNotes.explanation: The word “brother” recurs throughout verses 2–11, twice in this verse alone. The repetition presses the moral horror of the deed and anticipates God’s question, “Where is Abel thy brother?” The New Testament uses this story to show that hatred of a brother is murder in the heart.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Where is Abel thy brother?” The question recalls God’s first question to fallen humanity, “Where art thou?” (3:9). To Adam the LORD asked about Adam’s own place; to Cain He asks about his brother’s. The shift is significant: sin against God has become sin against one’s neighbor, and God holds the sinner accountable for both. Once more the question is an opening for confession. God knows where Abel lies, but He gives Cain a chance to speak the truth.

Cain’s answer moves beyond his father’s evasions. Adam had blamed the woman and, indirectly, God; Cain lies outright: “I know not.” Then he adds insolence: “Am I my brother’s keeper?” The retort is both falsehood and defiance. Having taken his brother’s life, he now disowns all responsibility for it. Murder has led to deceit, and deceit to contempt.

The word “keeper” carries irony. Abel was “a keeper of sheep” (verse 2), and the same Hebrew verb describes the charge given to Adam to keep the garden (2:15) and the LORD’s own care for His people: “The LORD is thy keeper” (Psalm 121:5). Cain mocks the very idea that he should watch over another. Scripture’s answer is plain. God commands, “Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself” (Leviticus 19:18), and Jesus made that love the measure of true religion (Luke 10:27–37).

The question still confronts every person. Indifference to a brother’s welfare is the soil in which Cain’s spirit grows. Those who belong to Christ cannot say that another’s life, faith, or suffering is none of their concern.

wordNotes.term: הֲשֹׁמֵר אָחִי אָנֹכִי (hashomer achi anokhi) — am I my brother’s keeper
wordNotes.explanation: Shomer is the participle of shamar, “to guard, watch over, keep.” It is used of Adam keeping the garden and of the LORD as the keeper of Israel. Cain’s question rejects the duty of care that belongs to family and covenant life. His sarcasm mirrors Abel’s occupation as a keeper of sheep.

verses.bibleText: And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God now sets aside indirect questions and confronts Cain with the deed itself: “What hast thou done?” The same words were spoken to Eve (3:13), but here they carry the full weight of knowledge. Nothing has escaped the LORD. Cain had sought a place where no one would see, but the Creator of life sees everything, and He is not indifferent when life is taken.

“The voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.” In Hebrew “blood” is plural, perhaps pointing to blood spilled in many places or to the life and descendants lost along with Abel. Blood stands for life (Leviticus 17:11), and life belongs to God. The verb “crieth” is the word used for the outcry of the oppressed calling for justice, as when Israel cried out in Egypt (Exodus 3:7) or when the outcry of Sodom rose before the LORD (18:20–21). Though Cain refused to speak the truth, the ground itself testified against him.

This cry is a vivid personification and should be read as such. Abel was not conscious in some other realm pleading for vengeance. Scripture teaches that “the dead know not any thing” (Ecclesiastes 9:5); Abel rests in death until the resurrection. What cries out is the fact of innocent blood unavenged, a wrong that God cannot ignore. In a similar way Revelation pictures the blood of martyrs beneath the altar calling for judgment (Revelation 6:9–10), a symbolic scene assuring God’s people that He has not forgotten them.

Jesus spoke of “the blood of righteous Abel” as the first in a long line of innocent blood shed by those who resisted God (Matthew 23:35). Hebrews adds that Abel “being dead yet speaketh” through his faith (Hebrews 11:4), and it contrasts his blood with that of Jesus, “the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24). Abel’s blood calls for justice; Christ’s blood speaks of mercy and pardon, even for those who shed it. The cross does not silence God’s justice but satisfies it, so that the guilty may be forgiven.

The verse comforts all who suffer wrong in silence. No injustice is hidden from God. He hears what the world ignores, and in His time He will set every wrong right.

wordNotes.term: קוֹל דְּמֵי אָחִיךָ (qol deme achikha) — the voice of thy brother’s blood
wordNotes.explanation: Deme is the plural of dam, “blood.” Hebrew often uses the plural for shed blood, particularly blood shed by violence, and the plural here underlines the crime. Blood represents life, which belongs to God, so its shedding is an offense He will answer.

wordNotes.term: צֹעֲקִים (tso‘aqim) — crieth
wordNotes.explanation: The verb tsa‘aq describes an outcry for help or justice from the wronged. It is used of Israel’s groaning in Egypt and of the outcry against Sodom. Applied to blood, it personifies the demand of innocent life for a just response from God.

verses.bibleText: And now art thou cursed from the earth, which hath opened her mouth to receive thy brother's blood from thy hand;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
For the first time a human being comes under a divine curse. In Genesis 3 the serpent was cursed and the ground was cursed for Adam’s sake, but Adam and Eve themselves were not. Now Cain stands beside the serpent as one directly cursed, for he has acted in the serpent’s spirit and shed his brother’s blood.

“Cursed from the earth” can be read in more than one way. It may mean that Cain is banished from the cultivated ground he once worked, or that he is cursed more than the ground. Verse 12 explains the practical result: the earth will resist him. The ground that Cain had tilled and whose fruit he had offered to God has “opened her mouth to receive thy brother’s blood from thy hand.” The image is stark. The soil swallowed the evidence, and now it becomes a witness and an adversary.

The phrase “from thy hand” lays the guilt squarely on Cain. The earth received the blood, but Cain’s hand shed it. Scripture repeatedly connects the moral condition of people with the condition of the land. Bloodshed pollutes the land (Numbers 35:33), and nations that defile it are said to be vomited out of it (Leviticus 18:28). Creation itself groans under human sin (Romans 8:22) and waits for the day of restoration.

wordNotes.term: אָרוּר אָתָּה מִן־הָאֲדָמָה (arur attah min-ha’adamah) — thou art cursed from the earth
wordNotes.explanation: Arur, “cursed,” is the same form pronounced on the serpent in Genesis 3:14. The preposition min may express separation (“banished from the ground”) or comparison (“more cursed than the ground”). Either way, Cain’s relationship with the soil he worked is broken, and the curse now rests on him personally.

verses.bibleText: When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The sentence strikes at Cain’s livelihood and his place in the world. “When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength.” Adam had been told he would eat by the sweat of his face from a ground bearing thorns (3:17–19). Cain’s judgment is heavier still. The farmer will find that the soil withholds its strength from him. The ground that drank his brother’s blood will not reward his labor.

“A fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth.” The two Hebrew words sound alike, na‘ wanad, and together they describe a life of restless wandering without home or security. Cain had been a settled tiller of the soil; now he will be an outcast, moving from place to place, unable to put down roots. The punishment fits the crime. He who destroyed his brother’s life and severed the bonds of family will himself live cut off from belonging.

Yet even this judgment falls short of death. The penalty for murder would later be life for life (9:6), but here God spares Cain’s life and leaves room for repentance. Mercy is mingled with justice, though Cain will not receive it as mercy.

wordNotes.term: נָע וָנָד (na‘ wanad) — a fugitive and a vagabond
wordNotes.explanation: The paired participles come from verbs meaning to wander, waver, and move aimlessly. Their similar sound strengthens the picture of a restless, unsettled life. The second word anticipates the land of Nod (verse 16), whose name means wandering.

verses.bibleText: And Cain said unto the LORD, My punishment is greater than I can bear.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Cain’s first words after the sentence are a complaint: “My punishment is greater than I can bear.” The defiance of verse 9 has collapsed into despair, but despair is not repentance. He says nothing about his brother, offers no admission of guilt, and asks for no forgiveness. His concern is the weight of what will happen to him.

The Hebrew word rendered “punishment” is ‘awon, which ordinarily means iniquity or guilt and can also denote the penalty that guilt brings. That double sense gives Cain’s words an unintended irony. He means that his sentence is too heavy, yet the phrase can also be heard as “my iniquity is too great to be borne away.” The verb “bear” is the same root used in verse 7 for the “lifting up” God had offered him. Cain had been offered acceptance, the removal of his guilt, if he would do well. Having refused it, he now finds his guilt crushing.

The contrast with true repentance is sharp. David, guilty of adultery and murder, cried, “Against thee, thee only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:4), and he found pardon. Paul distinguishes “godly sorrow” that “worketh repentance to salvation” from “the sorrow of the world” that “worketh death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). Cain shows the second kind. He regrets the consequences, not the sin. Yet even now God will answer him with mercy.

wordNotes.term: גָּדוֹל עֲוֹנִי מִנְּשֹׂא (gadol avoni minneso) — my punishment is greater than I can bear
wordNotes.explanation: ‘Awon means iniquity and, by extension, the guilt and penalty attached to it. Nasa’ means to lift, carry, or bear, and is often used of God bearing away sin. The phrase can therefore mean “my punishment is too heavy to carry” or “my iniquity is too great to be forgiven.” The context shows that Cain is lamenting his sentence rather than confessing his sin.

verses.bibleText: Behold, thou hast driven me out this day from the face of the earth; and from thy face shall I be hid; and I shall be a fugitive and a vagabond in the earth; and it shall come to pass, that every one that findeth me shall slay me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Cain lays out the consequences as he sees them. “Thou hast driven me out this day from the face of the earth” uses the same verb that described God driving Adam and Eve from the garden (3:24). The pattern of Genesis 3 repeats, but the distance grows. The parents were sent out of Eden; the son is driven from the cultivated ground and from settled life.

“From thy face shall I be hid.” Cain recognizes that his banishment involves separation from the presence of God. The tragedy is that he blames God for a distance his own choices created. God had come to him, questioned him, and pleaded with him. Cain had chosen anger, murder, and lies. Isaiah later names the real cause of such separation: “your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you” (Isaiah 59:2).

His greatest fear is that “every one that findeth me shall slay me.” The question naturally arises: who else was there? Genesis 5:4 states that Adam “begat sons and daughters,” and the narrative of chapter 4 covers a long span of time. Cain could expect that Abel’s blood relatives, the growing family of Adam, might seek to avenge the murder. The murderer now dreads becoming a victim himself. He who denied being his brother’s keeper finds no one willing to keep him.

Cain’s fear also shows that conscience had not died in him. He knew that bloodshed deserved death. Yet his knowledge produced terror rather than turning, and his words remain centered entirely on himself.

wordNotes.term: גֵּרַשְׁתָּ (gerashta) — thou hast driven me out
wordNotes.explanation: The verb garash means to drive out or expel, and is used of God driving the man from Eden and later of driving out the nations from Canaan. Cain applies to himself the language of his parents’ expulsion, now with a sense of more distant exile.

wordNotes.term: וּמִפָּנֶיךָ אֶסָּתֵר (umippaneykha essater) — and from thy face shall I be hid
wordNotes.explanation: The verb satar means to conceal or be hidden. Elsewhere God’s hiding of His face signals withdrawn favor and protection. Cain expects to live outside the sphere of God’s watchful care, which he associates with the cultivated land.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD said unto him, Therefore whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold. And the LORD set a mark upon Cain, lest any finding him should kill him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God answers Cain’s fear with an act of protection. “Therefore whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold.” The opening word is difficult in Hebrew; the ancient Greek, Syriac, and Latin translations read it as “Not so,” a direct reply to Cain’s claim that anyone who found him would kill him. Either reading conveys the same assurance. The LORD reserves vengeance to Himself and forbids private retaliation.

“Sevenfold” expresses full and severe punishment. Seven in Scripture signals completeness, and a sevenfold penalty is a thorough one (Leviticus 26:18; Psalm 79:12). The warning restrains the cycle of blood revenge before it can begin. Justice belongs to God, as Paul would later write: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Romans 12:19).

“The LORD set a mark upon Cain.” The text does not describe the mark. It may have been a visible sign on his person, or it may have been a sign given to Cain as a pledge of God’s protection, as later signs were given to Noah or to Gideon. Its purpose is stated: “lest any finding him should kill him.” It was a token of temporary protection, not of forgiveness or acceptance, and it has nothing to do with race or skin color, as some have wrongly taught in the past. Such ideas have no basis in the text and have caused grievous harm.

Why would God protect a murderer? The answer lies in His patience and His larger purposes. God allowed Cain to live, giving him time and opportunity to turn, just as He gives the world time before the final judgment (2 Peter 3:9). Jesus taught that the wheat and the tares must grow together until the harvest (Matthew 13:30). The life of Cain and his descendants would display the outworking of sin before the universe, so that when God finally judges, His justice will be evident to all. Divine restraint is not approval; it is mercy holding back the full consequences of rebellion until the appointed time.

wordNotes.term: אוֹת (’ot) — a mark
wordNotes.explanation: The word means a sign, token, or signal. It is used of the rainbow, of circumcision, of the Sabbath, and of the blood on the doorposts at Passover. An ’ot points beyond itself to a truth or pledge. Here it pledges God’s protection over Cain’s life without implying pardon.

wordNotes.term: שִׁבְעָתַיִם (shiv‘atayim) — sevenfold
wordNotes.explanation: The dual form of the number seven expresses a sevenfold measure, meaning complete and thorough recompense. Lamech will distort this protective decree into a boast of seventy-sevenfold revenge (verse 24).

verses.bibleText: And Cain went out from the presence of the LORD, and dwelt in the land of Nod, on the east of Eden.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Cain went out from the presence of the LORD.” The verse reads like a final departure. The phrase recalls Jonah fleeing “from the presence of the LORD” (Jonah 1:3), but Cain’s leaving is more settled. He goes not in repentance but under the weight of displeasure, and the narrative never again records any word between Cain and God.

He settles “in the land of Nod.” Nod means “wandering,” the same root as the word “vagabond” in verses 12 and 14. The sentence is fulfilled in the very name of his dwelling place. The wanderer lives in the land of wandering. The location cannot be identified on any map, and that seems fitting; it is the country of those who have no abiding home with God.

“On the east of Eden” continues a pattern. The cherubim guarded the east of the garden (3:24), and later the builders of Babel journey from the east (11:2). Movement eastward in these chapters often marks movement away from God’s presence. Cain goes farther from the place of fellowship than his parents did.

The verse warns that a person can stand near God, hear His voice, and still walk away. Yet God’s presence is never finally withdrawn from those who seek Him. The psalmist rejoiced that God is near even in the farthest places (Psalm 139:7–10), and the prodigal who journeyed into a far country found the father waiting when he returned (Luke 15:20).

wordNotes.term: נוֹד (Nod) — Nod
wordNotes.explanation: The name means “wandering” and shares its root with nad, “vagabond,” in verses 12 and 14. The land is named for the condition of its inhabitant. The narrator thus shows God’s sentence taking effect: Cain, condemned to wander, settles in the land of wandering.

verses.bibleText: And Cain knew his wife; and she conceived, and bare Enoch: and he builded a city, and called the name of the city, after the name of his son, Enoch.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Cain’s wife appears without introduction. She was almost certainly one of Adam’s daughters (5:4), since the first generations had no other possibility of marriage. Such unions were later forbidden in the law (Leviticus 18:9), when the human family had grown, but they were not wrong at the beginning. Abraham himself would marry his half sister (20:12). The question that has troubled many readers has a simple answer in the text: all humanity descends from one couple (Acts 17:26).

God’s kindness continues even toward the guilty. Cain receives a wife and a son, Enoch. The Lord “maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good” (Matthew 5:45), and family life is among the gifts He grants to all. The name Enoch probably means “dedicated” or “initiated.” The same root is used for dedicating a house or an altar.

“And he builded a city.” The Hebrew suggests he was engaged in building, perhaps a fortified settlement rather than a city in the later sense. The irony is plain. The man sentenced to wander builds a permanent place. Perhaps he sought by walls the security he did not trust God’s mark to provide. Perhaps he sought to defy his sentence. In either case Cain’s response to exile is self-reliance. He names the city after his son, establishing a name and a legacy apart from God.

The first city in Scripture is founded by the first murderer. That does not make cities evil in themselves; the Bible’s story ends in a city, the new Jerusalem, whose builder and maker is God (Hebrews 11:10; Revelation 21:2). The question is who builds and for whose glory. Cain’s city looks forward to Babel (11:4), where people say, “let us make us a name.” The godly line, by contrast, looks for “a city which hath foundations.”

wordNotes.term: עִיר (‘ir) — a city
wordNotes.explanation: The word covers any permanent settlement protected by a wall or fortification, from a small enclosure to a large town. Here it marks a shift from wandering to settled life. Scripture later contrasts cities built for human glory with the city God prepares for His people.

wordNotes.term: חֲנוֹךְ (Chanokh) — Enoch
wordNotes.explanation: The name is related to chanakh, “to dedicate, train, initiate,” a verb used for dedicating a house, the altar, or the temple. Cain dedicates his city in his son’s name, but God is not mentioned. The same name later belongs to Seth’s descendant who walked with God (5:24).

verses.bibleText: And unto Enoch was born Irad: and Irad begat Mehujael: and Mehujael begat Methusael: and Methusael begat Lamech.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The genealogy moves quickly through four generations: Irad, Mehujael, Methusael, and Lamech. Little is told of the middle names. They are links in a chain, preserved to show that Cain’s line continued and multiplied under God’s common providence.

Several of these names resemble names in Seth’s line in Genesis 5, such as Irad and Jared, Methusael and Methuselah, and the two Enochs and Lamechs. The similarity is in sound only; the spellings and meanings differ, and the characters stand in deliberate contrast. Counting from Adam, Lamech of Cain’s line is the seventh generation, as is Enoch of Seth’s line. One seventh boasts of killing; the other walks with God and does not see death (Hebrews 11:5).

wordNotes.term: וְעִירָד יָלַד (we‘irad yalad) — and Irad begat
wordNotes.explanation: Yalad, “to beget, bear,” is the standard verb of genealogies. Its repetition gives the list a steady rhythm. The same rhythm in Genesis 5 will trace the line of promise, inviting readers to compare the two family trees and their outcomes.

verses.bibleText: And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Lamech took unto him two wives.” With this brief notice the narrator records the first departure from the marriage pattern established at creation. God had made one woman for the man, and the two were to become “one flesh” (2:24). Lamech takes for himself, in the language of acquiring, two wives. The phrase “unto him” highlights self-interest: marriage has become a matter of what he wants.

Scripture often records polygamy without explicit comment, yet the narratives that follow, in the homes of Abraham, Jacob, Elkanah, and David, display its bitter fruit of rivalry, jealousy, and grief. Jesus later pointed back to the beginning as the standard: “from the beginning it was not so” (Matthew 19:8). The names of the wives, Adah, perhaps “ornament,” and Zillah, perhaps “shade” or “tinkling,” may reflect a culture valuing adornment and pleasure, though their exact meanings are uncertain.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּקַּח־לוֹ לֶמֶךְ שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים (wayyiqqach-lo lemekh shete nashim) — and Lamech took unto him two wives
wordNotes.explanation: Laqach, “to take,” is a common verb for taking a wife. The added “unto him” (lo) emphasizes Lamech’s initiative and self-interest. The number two openly contradicts the pattern of one man and one woman in Genesis 2:24.

verses.bibleText: And Adah bare Jabal: he was the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as have cattle.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jabal is called “the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as have cattle.” “Father” here means founder or originator, the first of a way of life. Abel had kept sheep, but Jabal developed a broader form of herding, moving with his livestock and living in tents. The word for cattle covers all kinds of domestic animals and was a measure of wealth.

The achievement is real. The cultural mandate to rule and work the earth (1:28) continues even in a line estranged from God. Skill and invention are gifts of the Creator, and they appear among the unbelieving as well as the faithful. Later, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob would live in tents as pilgrims (Hebrews 11:9), using the same way of life for a very different purpose.

wordNotes.term: מִקְנֶה (miqneh) — cattle
wordNotes.explanation: From qanah, “to acquire,” the word means livestock as a possession, including sheep, goats, cattle, and other animals. It is broader than tso’n, the flock Abel kept, and shows the expansion of herding into a source of wealth.

verses.bibleText: And his brother's name was Jubal: he was the father of all such as handle the harp and organ.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jubal is “the father of all such as handle the harp and organ.” The “harp” (kinnor) was a lyre with strings stretched over a frame, and the “organ” (‘ugav) was most likely a pipe or flute, an instrument still played by shepherds in the region. Music, in other words, is as old as human civilization.

That music appears first in Cain’s line does not make it suspect. The same lyre would be played by David to calm Saul (1 Samuel 16:23) and to praise God in the psalms. The pipe joins the orchestra of praise in Psalm 150. Gifts first developed by those far from God can be redeemed for His glory. The question is always how they are used. Among the Cainites, art and invention flourished alongside pride and violence; in the worship of God’s people, the same instruments would sound His praise.

wordNotes.term: כִּנּוֹר וְעוּגָב (kinnor we‘ugav) — harp and organ
wordNotes.explanation: Kinnor names a stringed lyre, the instrument most often associated with David and temple praise. ‘Ugav appears to be a wind instrument such as a pipe or flute. The pairing represents stringed and wind instruments, the beginnings of music in general.

verses.bibleText: And Zillah, she also bare Tubal-cain, an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron: and the sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Zillah bears Tubal-cain, “an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron.” The Hebrew describes him as a hammerer or sharpener of bronze and iron tools. The earliest metalworking involved hammering and shaping, and iron objects, sometimes from meteoric iron, are found in very early levels of human civilization. The text presents metalworking as an antediluvian achievement, and early ancient remains give no reason to doubt it.

The KJV “brass” translates a word meaning copper or bronze. These metals made possible better tools for farming and building, but also sharper weapons. In Lamech’s family the skill of the forge stands right beside the song of violence in the next verse. Technology itself is morally neutral. In the hands of those who love God it builds and serves; in the hands of those who exalt themselves it can wound and destroy. The prophet’s vision of the age to come reverses Lamech’s world: swords are beaten into plowshares (Isaiah 2:4).

The sister of Tubal-cain, Naamah, is named without explanation. Her name means “pleasant” or “lovely.” Women are seldom named in ancient genealogies, so her inclusion may indicate that she was well known, though Scripture records nothing more about her.

wordNotes.term: לֹטֵשׁ כָּל־חֹרֵשׁ נְחֹשֶׁת וּבַרְזֶל (lotesh kol-choresh nechoshet uvarzel) — an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron
wordNotes.explanation: Lotesh is a participle from latash, “to hammer, sharpen, whet.” Choresh means a craftsman or engraver. Nechoshet denotes copper or bronze, and barzel is iron. The phrase pictures Tubal-cain as the originator of metal forging.

verses.bibleText: And Lamech said unto his wives, Adah and Zillah, Hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech: for I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Lamech speaks in poetry, the first poem recorded after the man’s joyful words over the woman in 2:23. The contrast could hardly be greater. Adam’s song celebrated companionship; Lamech’s celebrates bloodshed. He addresses his two wives formally: “Adah and Zillah, Hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech.” The parallel lines follow the pattern of Hebrew poetry, each repeating and intensifying the one before.

“I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt.” The KJV wording is obscure, but the Hebrew means that Lamech killed a man for wounding him, a young man for striking him. The response was grossly out of proportion to the offense. A wound or a bruise brought death. Whether “man” and “young man” refer to one victim or two, the point is the same: Lamech boasts that he answers injury with killing.

Cain had murdered in secret and then lied about it. Lamech kills openly and composes a song to celebrate it. Sin has grown bolder in a few generations. Where Cain feared that others would kill him, Lamech warns others that he will kill them first. The progression shows the downward pull of a life lived apart from God. The same family that produced herders, musicians, and smiths now uses its arts to glorify violence.

This song stands in contrast to the law of God, which demanded proportionate justice, “eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Exodus 21:24), as a restraint upon vengeance. Jesus went further, calling His followers not to resist evil with evil (Matthew 5:38–39). Lamech’s boast is the opposite of the gospel.

wordNotes.term: כִּי אִישׁ הָרַגְתִּי לְפִצְעִי (ki ish haragti lefits‘i) — for I have slain a man to my wounding
wordNotes.explanation: Harag is the verb used of Cain killing Abel (verse 8). Petsa‘ means a wound or bruise, and the preposition le here indicates cause: “for wounding me.” The parallel “a young man to my hurt” (lechabburati, “for my bruise”) intensifies the boast. Lamech claims to have repaid minor injury with death.

verses.bibleText: If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold.” Lamech twists God’s protective decree for Cain (verse 15) into a license for limitless revenge. God had promised to take vengeance on anyone who killed Cain, a warning meant to restrain bloodshed. Lamech seizes the principle for himself, removes God from it, and multiplies it beyond all measure. He will not wait for God to act; he will avenge himself, and far more fiercely than God ever threatened.

The spirit of Lamech sums up the culture of Cain’s line: self-sufficient, proud, and violent. It anticipates the condition of the world before the flood, when “the earth was filled with violence” (6:11). Culture and technology advanced, but righteousness did not. The sequence warns that human progress cannot save humanity from its own heart.

Jesus answered Lamech’s song directly. When Peter asked whether he should forgive his brother seven times, Jesus replied, “Until seventy times seven” (Matthew 18:22). The Greek rendering of Jesus’ words closely matches the Greek translation of Lamech’s number here. Lamech’s limitless revenge is overturned by Christ’s limitless forgiveness. Where Lamech multiplied vengeance, the kingdom of God multiplies mercy, because it is grounded in the mercy God first showed to sinners.

wordNotes.term: שִׁבְעִים וְשִׁבְעָה (shiv‘im weshiv‘ah) — seventy and sevenfold
wordNotes.explanation: The number means seventy-seven, a deliberate escalation of the “sevenfold” in verse 15. It expresses unlimited vengeance. The Septuagint renders it with the same Greek expression that appears in Matthew 18:22, where Jesus uses the number to describe unlimited forgiveness.

verses.bibleText: And Adam knew his wife again; and she bare a son, and called his name Seth: For God, said she, hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
After the dark progression from Cain to Lamech, the narrative returns to Adam and Eve. The words “Adam knew his wife again” echo the opening of the chapter (verse 1) and signal a new beginning. God had not abandoned His promise. Through all the violence of Cain’s line, He had been preserving another seed.

Eve names her son Seth, “For God, said she, hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew.” The name Seth sounds like the Hebrew verb “appointed” or “set,” the same verb God used when He said, “I will put enmity between thee and the woman” (3:15). The God who set enmity between the serpent and the woman now sets a new seed in Abel’s place. The word “seed” itself recalls the promise of the woman’s seed who would crush the serpent’s head.

Eve’s words at this birth differ from those at Cain’s. Then she said, “I have gotten a man.” Now she says, “God hath appointed me.” Her hope has been tested and purified by grief. She has learned that the promise depends on God’s appointing, not on her expectations. Her faith survives the loss of one son and the moral ruin of another. Seth is not the promised Deliverer, but he is the one through whom the line of promise will continue.

That line runs through Genesis 5 to Noah, through Shem to Abraham, through Judah to David, and finally to Christ. Luke traces the genealogy of Jesus back through “Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God” (Luke 3:38). Through Seth, God kept the way open for the coming of the Seed who would defeat the serpent and reverse the curse. When the promise seemed dead with Abel, God appointed another; when all hope seemed buried in Christ’s tomb, God raised Him from the dead. The God of Seth is the God of resurrection.

wordNotes.term: שֵׁת ... שָׁת־לִי (Shet ... shat-li) — Seth ... hath appointed me
wordNotes.explanation: The name Shet is linked by sound and sense to shat, from shit, “to put, set, appoint.” The same verb appears in Genesis 3:15: “I will put enmity.” Eve sees Seth as God’s appointed replacement for Abel. The connection ties Seth’s birth to the promise of the seed.

wordNotes.term: זֶרַע אַחֵר (zera‘ acher) — another seed
wordNotes.explanation: Zera‘ means seed and therefore offspring or descendants. It is the key word in the promise of Genesis 3:15 and in God’s later promises to Abraham. Paul notes that the promise to Abraham’s seed points supremely to Christ.

verses.bibleText: And to Seth, to him also there was born a son; and he called his name Enos: then began men to call upon the name of the LORD.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Seth’s son is named Enos (Enosh), another Hebrew word for “man” or “mankind,” often used in passages that stress human frailty and mortality: “As for man, his days are as grass” (Psalm 103:15). Whether or not the name was chosen with that meaning, it suits the moment. In a world where violence was spreading, the line of Seth was marked by dependence on God.

“Then began men to call upon the name of the LORD.” This does not mean that no one had worshiped God before; Abel had offered, and Adam and Eve knew the LORD. The phrase points to something new: public, organized worship, a community gathering to call on God by name. In later Scripture, calling on the name of the LORD describes both prayer and proclamation. Abraham built altars and “called upon the name of the LORD” (12:8), and the phrase marks both his worship and his witness among the nations.

The contrast with Cain’s line is intentional. In verses 17–24 the name of God does not appear; Cain’s descendants build cities, make tools, compose songs, and celebrate violence, but they do not call on God. The line of Seth, in contrast, is defined by worship. Two cultures now exist side by side, one building its name, the other calling on God’s name.

The verse anticipates the gospel. Joel declared, “whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered” (Joel 2:32), and Paul applied that promise to all who call upon Christ (Romans 10:13). From the days of Enos to the end of time, God’s people are those who call on His name, and they do so in a world that often ignores Him.

wordNotes.term: אֱנוֹשׁ (Enosh) — Enos
wordNotes.explanation: Enosh is a poetic word for man or mankind, often used in contexts emphasizing mortality and weakness. Its use as a name may reflect the awareness of human frailty that leads people to seek God. It should not be pressed to mean that Enos himself was weaker than others.

wordNotes.term: לִקְרֹא בְּשֵׁם יְהוָה (liqro beshem YHWH) — to call upon the name of the LORD
wordNotes.explanation: The idiom combines qara’, “to call,” with “the name of the LORD.” It describes invoking God in worship and prayer and can include proclaiming His name to others. It marks the beginning of a recognized community devoted to the LORD.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: Why does the first recorded act of worship lead to the first recorded murder?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God receives worshipers who come by faith in His appointed way, warns those who resist Him, restrains evil in mercy, and preserves a line of faith through which His promise advances.
importantTerms: call upon the name of the LORD
discussionQuestions: What does Hebrews 11:4 add to our understanding of why Abel’s offering was accepted?
How does God’s conversation with Cain in verses 6–7 reveal His patience before judgment?
In what ways does Cain’s response in verses 9–14 resemble and differ from Adam’s in Genesis 3?
What does the line of Cain show about human achievement apart from God?
Why is the chapter’s ending with Seth and public worship significant after so much violence?
commonMisunderstandings: God did not reject Cain because farming was inferior to herding; the issue was the worshiper’s faith and response to God’s revealed way.
The mark of Cain was a sign of protection, not a racial marker and not a token of forgiveness.
Cain’s wife does not require another race of people; Adam had other sons and daughters (Genesis 5:4).
The cultural achievements of Cain’s line are not evil in themselves; they become dangerous when used for self-exaltation.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Hold together God’s grace in warning, restraining, and preserving with the seriousness of sin that grows from wrong worship into violence.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Come to God by the way He has provided in Christ, master the sin that waits at the door through His help, and take up the care of your brother and sister.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Acceptance with God comes by faith in the sacrifice He provides, not by offerings of our own devising, and that faith shows itself in love toward others.
flow: Two brothers worship the same God but come in different ways.
Abel comes by faith with the firstlings of the flock, pointing to the Lamb God would provide.
Cain brings what he chooses, grows angry, and ignores God’s warning about sin at the door.
Unresolved anger toward God becomes hatred and murder toward a brother.
God still offers a better word through the blood of Jesus and calls every person to come by faith.
simpleIllustrations: A gift that ignores what the recipient has asked for says more about the giver’s will than his love.
A wild animal lying beside a doorway waits for the moment someone opens it; sin works the same way when anger is welcomed.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you come to God by the way He has provided in Jesus rather than by an offering of your own choosing?
cautions: Avoid suggesting that Cain was doomed from birth; God pleaded with him to do well.
Do not use the mark of Cain to support any idea of racial curse.
Keep the focus on grace rather than presenting Abel’s obedience as the ground of his acceptance.

reflectionQuestions: Am I coming to God on His terms, by faith in Christ, or offering Him what I prefer to give?
What anger or resentment is crouching at the door of my heart right now?
Where have I said, by my actions, “Am I my brother’s keeper?”
How do I respond when God questions me: with confession or with excuses?
In a culture that builds without God, how can I call upon the name of the LORD publicly?
